readerTitle: 7:40 a.m. Monday: the order system is down and the trucks come at 3
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (금속 부품 제조사의 주문·출고 소프트웨어 장애) · 회사, 인물, 수치 모두 설명용
insight: 위기 대응은 하나의 큰 결정이 아니다. 사실 확인, 알리기, 핵심 업무 지키기, 재발 막기를 순서대로 결정하는 일이다.
misconception: 위기가 오면 모두가 즉시 뛰어들어 모든 것을 평소처럼 되살리는 것이 최선이다. 끝나면 원인 업체만 바꾸면 된다.

sources.text: 리스크 관리와 사업 연속성의 일반 원칙 (위기 대응 책임자 지정, 핵심 업무 우선순위, 단일 장애점 제거)
모든 회사, 인물, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치(직원 60명, 주문 300건, 긴급 주문 40건, 장애 30시간)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 카드 간 숫자가 일치하는지 다시 확인하세요.
특정 국가의 법적 신고 의무(예: 데이터 유출 시 신고)는 다루지 않습니다. 이 시나리오는 데이터 유출이 아닌 공급업체 서비스 장애로 설정했습니다.
운송사의 웹 예약으로 라벨을 만드는 우회 방법은 일반적인 예시입니다. 실제 가능 여부는 운송사마다 다르므로 카드에 특정 업체를 적지 않았습니다.

cards.title: 7:40 a.m. Monday: the order system is down and the trucks come at 3
body: You run a 60-person company that makes metal fasteners for repair shops and factories. Every order, pick list and shipping label runs through one cloud software system.
This morning it won't load. The vendor's status page says "investigating." No time estimate. 300 orders are waiting, and the carrier's trucks arrive at 3 p.m.
You'll make four calls today. Each one builds on the last.

image.label: Warehouse at dawn with a frozen screen and an empty loading dock
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 이른 아침 창고. 포장대 위 모니터에 로딩 아이콘만 돌고, 뒤로 빈 출고장과 "3:00 PM" 시계. 직원 몇 명이 화면을 바라봄. 실제 소프트웨어나 운송사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Everyone is looking at you.
body: Staff are gathering by the packing tables. Your IT person is rebooting computers. A salesperson is already on the phone with a customer.

options.text: Wait for the vendor's fix and ask staff to stand by
options.feedback: You lose the morning hoping. If the fix takes a day, you'll face the 3 p.m. trucks with no plan and nothing packed.

options.text: Put one person in charge, gather facts for 30 minutes, then meet
options.feedback: You trade a little speed for a clear picture: what still works, which orders are urgent, what the vendor knows. One owner means one plan.

options.text: Let everyone jump in on their own: IT fixes, sales calls, warehouse improvises
options.feedback: The energy is real, but customers hear three different stories and two teams pick the same orders. Effort without a plan creates new problems.

cards.title: Say you put one person in charge. Now it's 9:00.
body: The facts: the outage hits many of the vendor's clients and could last a day. Of your 300 orders, 40 are for factories whose machines stop without your parts.

options.text: Call the 40 urgent customers and stay quiet with the rest
options.feedback: You protect the customers who matter most today. The other 260 find out when tracking never updates, and they wonder what else you didn't say.

options.text: Tell everyone now: what happened, what you know, what you don't, and when the next update comes
options.feedback: Admitting "we don't know yet" feels weak, but a promised noon update builds trust. Urgent customers can plan, and nobody is surprised.

options.text: Say it will be fixed by lunch so nobody panics
options.feedback: It calms people for three hours. Then you break a promise you never controlled, and every update after that is doubted.

cards.title: Say you told everyone. It's 10:30 and still down.
body: Your team finds a way around the system. The sales inbox holds every order confirmation. The carrier lets you book shipments and print labels on its own website.

options.text: Don't. Pause all shipping until the system is back
options.feedback: No mistakes, but nothing ships. Forty factories may stop their machines, and you lose a day you can't get back.

options.text: Run the 40 urgent orders on paper, hold the rest
options.feedback: Slower work on fewer orders keeps errors low and keeps your most critical customers running. The other 260 wait a day, as you already told them.

options.text: Push all 300 orders through on paper by 3 p.m.
options.feedback: Heroic, and some will ship. But rushed hand-written pick lists mean wrong parts, and a wrong part costs more than a late one.

cards.softwareNote: If you run a software business, the crisis is often your own outage. The same order applies: one person in charge, an honest status update with a next-update time, then keep the most critical features or customers working first.

cards.title: Say you shipped the 40. The system came back after 30 hours.
body: All 40 urgent orders arrived on time. The rest shipped a day late. Now your team wants to make sure this never hurts this much again.

options.text: Switch to a different software vendor
options.feedback: It might be more reliable, but switching is costly and any vendor can go down. You'd still have one system that everything depends on.

options.text: Keep the vendor, but build a backup: a daily export of open orders, a ready paper-process kit, and a practice run each quarter
options.feedback: Small, steady costs turn today's lucky improvising into a plan. The system can still fail, but the business no longer stops when it does.

options.text: Buy business interruption insurance and move on
options.feedback: Insurance may cover some lost money. It won't stop your customers' machines next time, and they're the ones who'll remember.

cards.title: Backups cost something too.
body: A paper process is slower and more error-prone. It works for 40 orders, not for 3,000. And a plan nobody has practiced tends to fail the day you need it.
Don't protect against everything. Weigh how likely a failure is against how much it would hurt. A system that runs every order deserves a backup. A rarely used report tool probably doesn't.

image.label: A simple backup kit on a shelf next to a calendar
image.brief: 선반 위에 "Backup kit" 상자: 출력된 주문 목록, 빈 피킹 리스트 양식, 연락처 카드. 옆 벽걸이 달력에 분기마다 "Practice" 표시. 차분한 색감, 로고 없음.

cards.title: A crisis is four decisions, in order.
body: Each call you made maps to an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1 → Crisis response:** one owner, facts before action
**Decision 2 → Crisis response:** say what you know, what you don't, and when you'll update
**Decision 3 → Keeping the business running:** protect the most critical work first
**Decision 4 → Single points of failure:** add a backup, sized by probability times impact
cards.callout: **Try it today:** name the one system or supplier your business can't run without. Write down what you'd do in the first hour if it failed.
